items.title: Noah’s Ark Researcher Reveals DEATH Threats, Stunning New Radar Findings
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Whoa.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The founder of an organization digging at a site in Turkey he believes could unveil the real-life Noah’s Ark has reportedly faced terrifying death threats and a burglary of his apartment.

Andrew Jones, founder of Noah’s Ark Scans, said it took years to get a permit from the Turkish government to be able to dig.

“For our efforts, it’s taken years, if not decades,” he said. “When you’re trying to get a permit, you have to work under a Turkish university, and it’s not just under the Turkish university; you’re working with a Turkish professor.”

Jones continued, “So here’s someone who’s going to say, ‘OK. I’m going to put my reputation on the line looking for Noah’s Ark, and then I’m going to go ahead and get go through the obstacles, and the time,’ and anything else being thrown at him or her to get a permit done.”

In addition to finding people willing to put their reputations on the line, Jones said you also need to have funding, which can be another barrier. Jones said he and his team had to act quickly once the permit was approved.

“It was the start of this year when we got the permit,” he said. “We had one month to basically fundraise, get organized, get people involved.”

Challenges still abound. The professor involved in the Noah’s Ark Scans project is reportedly being called a “traitor” to Turkey by some, with his atheist and agnostic friends also piling on.

Jones, too, has faced some challenges. He’s unsure whether the Noah’s Ark expedition sparked problems for him, but, months ago, he started having people pound on his door in the middle of the night earlier this year while issuing threats to kill him.

While motives are difficult to know, Jones said the chaos started after his team announced they received a permit.

“We made the mistake of announcing we had a permit,” he said. “In regards to like physical threats or robbery, I’ve never had that issue until this happened.”

The people pounding on the door in the middle of the night were “making threats and cursing in English.”

“They were targeting someone who they thought spoke English,” he said. “It wasn’t Turkish they were speaking. They were saying, ‘F you, and I’m going to kill you.'”

Jones called a friend to come over and examine the situation, but they never found the culprit. Then, just days later, it happened again. The Noah’s Ark Scans founder inevitably decided to leave the apartment altogether and stay with a friend out of abundance of caution.

His mission to find the Ark hasn’t stopped, and he has no plans to halt. Watch the video for the full story on where the expedition currently stands:

items.title: Alex Kendrick’s Blunt Message to Christians
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Encouraging.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Filmmaker Alex Kendrick is gearing up for a fascinating theatrical expedition as he and his brother, Stephen, prepare to return to their roots in a truly unique way.

In fact, the brothers are set to release, “Flywheel: Ignition of the Soul,” on Oct. 16, a remake of their popular 2003 movie, “Flywheel.”

“‘Flywheel’ was our very first movie shot in standard definition, not even high definition, over 20 years ago,” Alex Kendrick recently told CBN News. “And [I] kind of fell on my face thinking I could make a good feature film, and it turned out to be pretty low production quality.”

In fact, he said, he almost didn’t release the movie as he didn’t realize at the time how difficult filmmaking can be. Ultimately, though, the brothers proceeded — and the rest is history.

“The only thing I did right was beg God to use it,” Kendrick said. “And my brother Stephen helping me and saying, ‘We need to pray Ephesians 3:20 — that God would do exceedingly abundantly more than we could ask or imagine. So that’s the only thing we did right.”

Despite being green filmmakers at the time, the Kendricks were shocked to see how God showed up. “Flywheel” sold 1.3 million DVDs and had a massive response from audiences — much larger than they could have ever imagined.

“People said once they got over the production quality, like 10 minutes into it, then they were moved by the story, and they would come back and say, ‘I saw a version of myself on the screen,'” Kendrick said. “And the the Lord did what only the Lord can do by touching their hearts, and so we’ve always wanted to remake that, and higher quality over the years.”

That idea started coming to fruition two years ago, when the Kendricks were in Brazil releasing, “The Forge,” another faith-based film. The duo took some young Christian filmmakers through a boot camp and, through that experience and through prayer, the idea was birthed to work with teams there to remake, “Flywheel.”

“The Lord opened the door for us to remake, ‘Flywheel,'” he said. “We instantly got the funding, the support, the distribution, so we reshot it in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in Portuguese, and had wonderful cast and crew that love the Lord help us make it, and so it’s made in their culture, their language. They’re so thrilled about it.”

Kendrick said pre-screenings of the film have left audiences crying and cheering. The movie has now been dubbed for Americans audiences into English. Regardless of the language in which the film is viewed, Kendrick believes audiences will love it.

“This movie that talks about lordship and is now modernized [and] is coming out in theaters Oct. 16,” he said. “Can’t wait to see what the Lord does with this one.”

Kendrick believes this movie is releasing at the right cultural moment, with the main character working as a successful used car salesman when he goes through a very dark time in his life. This man realizes he needs more than his own logic to navigate it all, seeking help in marriage, fatherhood — and more. It’s his newfound faith in Jesus that changes everything.

“We do not need more lukewarm Christians,” Kendrick said. “What we need is Christians who are sold out and truly followers of Jesus Christ.”

He continued, “When people see the life of a Christian, what they don’t need to see is half-hearted commitment to our Savior, and half-hearted integrity. They need to see someone who lives for a higher purpose, because we serve an almighty God and that the way we live bears fruit of that relationship.”

Kendrick is hoping — much like the first “Flywheel” — people see themselves on the screen and confront spiritual issues in their own lives.

items.title: Greta Gerwig’s Narnia Looks Awesome: What We Saw and Heard at the IMAX Preview Event
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: Netflix released the first trailer for Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew on Tuesday afternoon. A few hours before that, RELEVANT got a first look at the movie at an exclusive IMAX sneak peek event in New York featuring an in-person interview between Stephen Colbert and writer-director Greta Gerwig. What
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Netflix released the first trailer for Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew on Tuesday afternoon. A few hours before that, RELEVANT got a first look at the movie at an exclusive IMAX sneak peek event in New York featuring an in-person interview between Stephen Colbert and writer-director Greta Gerwig. What we learned should put a lot of skeptical fans at ease.

Narnia fans had reasons to be nervous. Empire reported in September that Gerwig was approaching the film as a rock opera, with Meryl Streep voicing Aslan, the male lion who stands in for Christ in C.S. Lewis’ story. For people who grew up on these books, that was a lot to take in.

Gerwig explained those choices and why she wanted to begin her Narnia filmmaking with The Magician’s Nephew.

Gerwig grew up on Narnia. “I would not be who I am without these books,” she said. “They created me.”

“I don’t remember a time I didn’t know the books,” she said. “They were read to me before I could read.”

She loved the series so much that when the BBC aired its Narnia television adaptations, Gerwig’s parents, who didn’t have a TV at home, got one just so she could watch them.

The Narnia series has been, she said, “a part of the DNA of who I knew myself to be.”

And because of that, she said the film project “started from my complete love of these books.” Netflix brought her on before Barbie became a global phenomenon, when Lady Bird and Little Women were her two solo directing credits.

Narnia and Little Women, she said, are “the biggest books in my life.”

Her lifelong devotion to Lewis’ work shaped how she approached The Magician’s Nephew. And reading his memoir Surprised by Joy changed how she saw the story.

“I realized how much C.S. Lewis put his own story into The Magician’s Nephew,” she said. “He lost his own mother. And the intimacy Lewis had with the material drew me in.”

In the book, Digory Kirke’s mother is dying, and Aslan sends him home with an apple from Narnia for her. Lewis was nine when his own mother died of cancer.

While writing the script, Gerwig went to Oxford and Cambridge, trying “to align myself with where Lewis’ soul was.”

Colbert asked how Lewis’ faith connected with her own work. “Faith has been a thread through all of my work,” she said. “Lady Bird was born from my experience growing up in Catholic school. For me, film and faith have always gone hand in hand.”

Which brings us back to Aslan. Colbert didn’t directly ask about Streep, and Aslan doesn’t speak in the trailer. But someone involved with the film who has seen it and asked not to be named told RELEVANT that Aslan is clearly male. The voice, that person said, comes across as Aslan, not Streep. And considering Gerwig referred to Aslan as “he” throughout the conversation, no, the beloved character is not being re-gendered. So we can put that rumor to rest.

Gerwig also talked about the world she built around him. The Magician’s Nephew is an epic story that follows the creation of Narnia, but she wanted to keep Digory at the center of it.

“It’s always this way for me with movies,” she said. “It’s all about character. In vast worlds, the story can also be about what’s in a boy’s heart. It can be vast and it can be small.”

Music is a key part of that world: After all, in The Magician’s Nephew Aslan sings Narnia into existence. In Netflix’s announcement, Gerwig described “the gorgeously improbable but completely brilliant concept of a cosmic lion singing the world of Narnia to life.”

Her musical choices for the film are bold, and from what we saw, they work. Gerwig said she met with Led Zeppelin’s Robert Plant and Jimmy Page to get permission to use “Stairway to Heaven” in the film. They granted it. To her, the song directly connects to the Narnia story: a path toward heaven, with things on either side trying to pull you off it.

The film’s score is by Mark Ronson and Andrew Wyatt, who worked with her on Barbie. They started earlier in preproduction than usual, she said, because setting the music first helped her design the world.

Before the preview event, the rock-opera approach and Streep’s casting had dominated the conversation about The Magician’s Nephew. But after hearing Gerwig talk about the material, and her vision for the film, we trust her with it. Colbert, who has seen the film, opened the conversation by telling her, “I was so moved not only by the story, but the scope of the film. It was emotionally overwhelming.”

Lewis’ family is on board, too. In an Oct. 6 statement, the families of his stepsons, David and Douglas Gresham, said they had “personally witnessed her sincere passion for the Narnia series” during their visit to the set in London.

So why start with The Magician’s Nephew instead of The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe? Gerwig said she had seen a note from Lewis in which he favored people beginning with Narnia’s creation rather than following book publication order. So, she did.

For anyone who needs a refresher, The Magician’s Nephew, published in 1955, tells how Narnia is created through two children, Digory and Polly, who travel between worlds. Gerwig’s is the first film adaptation of the book. The cast includes David McKenna as Digory, Beatrice Campbell as Polly, Daniel Craig as Uncle Andrew, Emma Mackey as Jadis, Carey Mulligan, Ciarán Hinds and Meryl Streep, with Seamus McGarvey as director of photography. The series has sold more than 120 million copies.

Gerwig says Narnia created her. IMAX sneak previews begin Feb. 10, 2027, ahead of the Feb. 12 theatrical release. The film arrives on Netflix April 2.

items.title: On Being Tamed by Great Literature
items.author: Moira Gleason
items.summary:
Moira Gleason

"The Little Prince" quietly expresses just what we’re missing when we grow up and quit reading literature out of love.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Moira Gleason

The College Beat: ARTICLE XIX

. . .

When I open my phone, my Instagram feed offers me a list of five books I ought to read to become “disgustingly well educated” or “insufferable at dinner parties.” The first seems an oxymoron, and the second I could probably achieve on my own without reading anything.

Reading literature—especially physical books—has become a subculture. Reports abound with evidence of college students who cannot read a full book and aren’t being asked to do so. But as an English major and avid reader, I am unsatisfied with the Book Tok characterization of literature as an aesthetic or a lifehack to make you sound smart. I did not fully understand why until I read a French children’s book in my very last literature class of college.

Known for its childlike illustrations and subtle depth of thought, Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s The Little Prince tells the story of an aviator who crashes his plane in the Sahara Desert and meets a little boy who has journeyed to earth from another planet. In eighty-three pages, the little volume quietly expresses just what we’re missing when we grow up and quit reading literature out of love.

On his journey, the little prince meets a fox who tells him he cannot play with him because he has not yet been tamed. When the boy asks him what “tamed” means, the fox responds, “It’s something that’s been too often neglected. It means, ‘to create ties.’”

“For me you’re only a little boy just like a hundred thousand other little boys,” the fox continues. “And I have no need of you. And you have no need of me, either. For you I’m only a fox like a hundred thousand other foxes. But if you tame me, we’ll need each other.” 

The prince protests he does not have time to tame the fox. He has other things to learn. 

“The only things you learn are the things you tame,” the fox responds. “People haven’t time to learn anything. They buy things ready-made in stores. But since there are no stores where you can buy friends, people no longer have friends. If you want a friend, tame me!”

The little prince must be patient, the fox says. The process takes time. He must sit a little way away from him and then, day-by-day, return and sit a little closer.

He does, and somewhere along the way the two become friends, tied together. When they must part, the fox weeps.

Exupéry suggests a simple philosophy: Relationships create ties, and we become responsible for those things to which we are tied. 

At its most obvious level, Exupéry’s insight concerns love in human relationships. But the same dynamic applies to the act of reading literature. After all, to read well is to develop a relationship—to create ties—with an author, a story, and characters. 

This parallel didn’t sink in for me until I had to unpack my books from undergrad: The pages of War and Peace are dog-eared and annotated from three months of reading and rereading, the red dye has worn off the rounded corners of my complete works of William Shakespeare, and poor T. S. Eliot is now missing his cover completely. But when I look at them, I remember how each author moved me and informed my vision of the world—and for a moment I feel that movement again. 

These great authors tamed me, in a way. The pages bear the evidence of the time and patient effort I offered to the books. In turn, each volume shaped my heart in subtle ways.

It’s a romantic idea, but a true one. When you read something, it becomes part of you and informs the way you approach people and ideas. The process seems obvious in children. As a child, books like Anne of Green Gables and Little House on the Prairie filled my imaginations and shaped my desires.

Then we grow up. If we read at all, it is likely out of a vague sense of duty or for practical purposes.

But engaging with literature is not about cultivating an aesthetic or cramming information into your head to regurgitate at parties. It’s a process of love—taking the time to approach the mind of an author with humility, prepared to be moved and create ties. When we stop reading literature, we risk losing that capacity altogether.

items.title: Wednesday, October 14, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, the scribes and Pharisees make Jesus a scapegoat: They “began to act with hostility toward him and to interrogate him about many things, for they were plotting to catch him at something he might say.”
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Galatians 5:18-25

But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not subject to the law. Now the works of the flesh are obvious: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, drunkenness, carousing, and things like these. I am warning you, as I warned you before: those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

By contrast, the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. There is no law against such things. And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. If we live by the Spirit, let us also be guided by the Spirit.

Psalm
Psalm 1:1-2, 3, 4, 6

Happy are those
    who do not follow the advice of the wicked,
or take the path that sinners tread,
    or sit in the seat of scoffers;
but their delight is in the law of the Lord,
    and on his law they meditate day and night.
They are like trees
    planted by streams of water,
which yield their fruit in its season,
    and their leaves do not wither.
In all that they do, they prosper.
The wicked are not so,
    but are like chaff that the wind drives away.
for the Lord watches over the way of the righteous,
    but the way of the wicked will perish.

Gospel Reading
Luke 11:42-46

“But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and herbs of all kinds, and neglect justice and the love of God; it is these you ought to have practiced, without neglecting the others. Woe to you Pharisees! For you love to have the seat of honor in the synagogues and to be greeted with respect in the marketplaces. Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without realizing it.”

One of the lawyers answered him, “Teacher, when you say these things, you insult us too.” And he said, “Woe also to you lawyers! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not lift a finger to ease them.

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, the scribes and Pharisees make Jesus a scapegoat: They “began to act with hostility toward him and to interrogate him about many things, for they were plotting to catch him at something he might say.” 

René Girard, the great Franco-American philosopher and social commentator, is best known for his speculations on what he called the scapegoating mechanism. Sadly, Girard maintained, most human communities are predicated upon this dysfunctional and deeply destructive instinct. Roughly speaking, it unfolds as follows. When tensions arise in a group, people commence to cast about for a scapegoat, for someone or some group to blame. Deeply attractive, even addictive, the scapegoating move rapidly attracts a crowd, which in short order becomes a mob.

In their common hatred of the victim, the blamers feel an ersatz sense of togetherness. Filled with the excitement born of self-righteousness, the mob then endeavors to isolate and finally eliminate the scapegoat, convinced that this will restore order to their roiled society. The Gospels appreciated the Girardian dynamic long before Girard.
